title_en: Fragments on the Letter to the Galatians
author: Eusebius of Emesa
occasion: Eusebius explains Paul's letter to the Galatians, beginning from the report that some from the circumcision party went out and persuaded the nations to judaize, contrary to the apostolic decree and the Holy Spirit. He defends Paul's gospel of grace against those who would impose Jewish observances.
argument: Eusebius argues that the Galatian crisis arose when some from the circumcision party persuaded Gentile believers to judaize, contrary to the apostolic decree and the Holy Spirit. He insists that Christ alone died for the world, and that Paul's gospel, preached in the power of the Holy Spirit, sets believers outside the law. The law was given because of transgressions to train the mind and expose sin, but its bodily observances are dead for the believer, and baptism clothes all alike with Christ, making grace common to Jew and Greek, male and female. Paul's so-called allegory of Hagar and Sarah is a prophecy enacted through historical events, showing that Sinai and the present Jerusalem belong to slavery, while the heavenly citizenship brings freedom. Eusebius concludes that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision matters, but only the new creation in Christ.

outline.move: Introduces the Galatian problem of judaizing and comments on Galatians 1:4–2:16, showing that Christ alone saves, Paul's gospel is from the Spirit, and justification comes by faith rather than works of the law.

Explains Galatians 2:18–4:10, arguing that the law's bodily observances are dead for the believer, the law was added because of transgressions to train the mind, baptism unites all in Christ, and returning to calendar observances is a form of idolatry.

Comments on Galatians 4:12–24, defending Paul's affectionate tone, explaining the 'allegory' as a prophecy enacted through historical events, and distinguishing it from figurative allegory such as in the Song of Songs.

Concludes with Galatians 4:25–6:15, linking Sinai and Hagar to slavery and the present Jerusalem, explaining why Paul mentions sin when discussing the law, and affirming that only the new creation in Christ matters.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of the letter to the Galatians, whose gospel of grace Eusebius defends.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle whom Paul confronted at Antioch; Eusebius says Peter undermined by his own conduct the decree that had been sent from the apostles to Antioch and the whole world.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: The lawgiver through whom the law was given at Sinai; Eusebius says he did not die for the world.

cast.name: Ishmael
cast.who: Son of Hagar, ancestor of the Hagarenes who dwell near Sinai.

cast.name: Jeremiah
cast.who: The prophet who enacted a prophecy with a linen waistcloth buried at the Euphrates.

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Quotations from the letter to the Galatians are introduced by phrases such as φησίν or given as lemma before comment.

voices.speaker: Paul's opponents (paraphrased)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by λεγόντων or described as those who distort the gospel.

voices.speaker: Scripture (Song of Songs, Jeremiah)
voices.how_marked: Quoted or alluded to with phrases such as ὡς τὸ or τὸ ῥηθέν.

key_terms.sense: The Mosaic law with its bodily observances such as food rules, Sabbath, and circumcision, which Eusebius says cannot save and has ceased for believers.
God's grace in Christ, contrasted with the law as the perfect and life-giving gift that frees believers from bodily observances.
Works required by the law, especially bodily observances, which Eusebius says are difficult and cannot justify, unlike faith.
Faith in Christ, the easy and great way of righteousness that replaces the law's difficult works.
In Paul's usage, a prophecy enacted through historical events, not a figurative reading that disregards the literal sense.
The weak and poor elements of the world, such as calendar observances, which cannot enrich or lead to true piety.
Slavery under the law and earthly concerns, contrasted with the freedom of the heavenly citizenship.
The freedom that comes from the heavenly citizenship in Christ, released from earthly cares and the law's bonds.
The new creation in Christ, which alone matters, making circumcision and uncircumcision irrelevant.
Circumcision, the chief bodily mark of the law, which Eusebius says no longer has any power for those in Christ.
Uncircumcision, the Gentile state, which also has no power in the new creation.
The Jewish way of life under the law, which Paul zealously defended before his conversion.
The Christian faith, which Paul persecuted before his conversion.
A commandment, distinguished from works of the law; Eusebius says a commandment justifies when heard, while works are hard to achieve.

scripture: Eusebius cites the Septuagint and refers to Old Testament books by their Greek titles, such as the Song of Songs (Ἄσματα τῶν Ἀσμάτων). He quotes the virgin prophecy without naming Isaiah and Jeremiah's waistcloth prophecy. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names: Song of Songs, Jeremiah. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint where applicable.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain; the mid-4th century is inferred from Eusebius of Emesa's lifetime.
The original extent and arrangement of the fragments is uncertain, since they survive only in catena excerpts.
Whether Eusebius wrote a continuous commentary or separate homilies on Galatians is uncertain.
Hagar herself is not named in the extant fragments; only her descendants, the Hagarenes, are mentioned.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Peter undermined by his own conduct the decree that had been sent from the apostles to Antioch and the whole world
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πρὸς τὸν Πέτρον ὁ λόγος· σὺ κατέλυσας αὐτὰ δόγματι ὅπερ ἀπεστάλη παρ' ὑμῶν τοῖς Ἀντιοχεῦσι καὶ πάσῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Peter is addressed; the text says 'you dissolved these things by a decree' (σὺ κατέλυσας αὐτὰ δόγματι), not that he undermined a decree sent from the apostles. The syntax is difficult, but δόγματι is instrumental ('by a decree/decision'), not a reference to a decree sent from the apostles. The phrase 'παρ' ὑμῶν' likely refers to Paul and Barnabas or the Antiochene church, not 'from the apostles' as a group.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Ishmael: Son of Hagar, ancestor of the Hagarenes who dwell near Sinai
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οἱ Ἀγαρηνοὶ οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰσμαὴλ τὴν ἔρημον ἔχουσι τὴν παρατείνουσαν ἕως τοῦ Σινᾶ ὄρους
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text mentions Ishmael only as the ancestor from whom the Hagarenes descend; Ishmael himself is not a character in the commentary. The Hagarenes are the ones who 'have the desert extending to Mount Sinai.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul's opponents (paraphrased): Introduced by λεγόντων or described as those who distort the gospel
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπείσθησαν δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν διαστρεφόντων λεγόντων, ὡς οἱ λοιποὶ ἀπόστολοι οὐ κωλύουσι τοὺς βουλομένους τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opponents are introduced by a participial phrase (τῶν διαστρεφόντων λεγόντων) describing those who 'distort' and 'say,' but they are not given direct speech; rather, their claim is reported in indirect statement with ὡς. They are not 'paraphrased' in the sense of having their voice represented distinctly.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Hagar herself is not named in the extant fragments; only her descendants, the Hagarenes, are mentioned
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἡ γὰρ ἀλληγορία... οἷόν ἐστι τὸ φιλησάτω με ἀπὸ φιλημάτων στόματος αὐτοῦ, τοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The uncertainty note is correct that Hagar is not named, but this belongs in 'uncertain' not 'names.' However, the claim is actually correct—Hagar is not named. The error is elsewhere: the brief's 'names' section includes 'Song of Songs' with Greek form Ἄσματα τῶν Ἀσμάτων, but the source has the genitive form τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων (dative plural with article), which should be noted.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul's so-called allegory of Hagar and Sarah is a prophecy enacted through historical events
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Νῦν τῷ ὀνόματι κατεχρήσατο, οὐ τῇ δυνάμει τῆς ἀλληγορίας... ἡ οὖν δι' ἔργων προφητεία ἀλληγορία νῦν ὠνόμασται
_unresolved_facts.fix: Eusebius says Paul 'abused/misused the name' (κατεχρήσατο) of allegory, not that it 'is' a prophecy enacted through events. He distinguishes this from 'true' allegory (as in Song of Songs) and calls it a 'prophecy through deeds' (δι' ἔργων προφητεία) that was 'named allegory' (ἀλληγορία νῦν ὠνόμασται)—a terminological point, not an identification of what allegory essentially is.

_unresolved_facts.claim: baptism clothes all alike with Christ, making grace common to Jew and Greek, male and female
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὐχ ἡ τοῦ νόμου τήρησις, φησί, βελτίονας ποιεῖ τοὺς πιστεύσαντας τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν τοὺς Ἰουδαίους, ἀλλ' ἡ δύναμις τοῦ βαπτίσματος τὸ Χριστὸν ἐνδύσασθαι παρέχουσα, κοινὴν ποιεῖ τὴν χάριν πάντων ὁμοῦ, βαρβάρων, Ἑλλήνων, Ἰουδαίων, θήλεος, ἄρρενος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says baptism's power 'to clothe with Christ' makes grace common (κοινὴν ποιεῖ τὴν χάριν), not that baptism 'clothes all alike with Christ'—the infinitive τὸ Χριστὸν ἐνδύσασθαι is the content of what baptism provides, not the mechanism of equalization. The equalization is the result (κοινὴν ποιεῖ τὴν χάριν).

_unresolved_facts.claim: He defends Paul's gospel of grace against those who would impose Jewish observances
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source is a catena fragment collection of exegetical comments, not a sustained defense. Eusebius explains Paul's letter verse by verse; there is no explicit 'defense' frame or polemical stance attributed to Eusebius himself beyond standard exegesis.
